title: everything happens for a reason
hook: the line everyone says after a breakup, and nobody can source

segments.voice: Everything happens for a reason. It gets said after a breakup, a missed flight, a job that fell through. It's on mugs and in captions. It often gets pinned on Aristotle, but you won't find the line in anything he wrote. So where does it come from, and why does it feel so true, even to people who aren't sure what they believe?
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `NOT ARISTOTLE.` → `SO WHERE'S IT FROM?`

segments.voice: Start with the mind. Researchers asked young children why rocks are pointy: because of how they formed, or so animals could scratch on them? Many picked the animals. Children see purpose everywhere, and adults never fully grow out of it. In one set of studies, adults were asked about big events in their own lives. Believers often said those events happened for a reason, and so did a surprising number of atheists. A mind that's always reading other people's intentions starts reading them into events, too. Then the old ideas. Aristotle wrote that nature does nothing in vain: an eye is for seeing. That's about how living things are built, not about your breakup. The Stoics went further and saw the whole universe ordered by reason. Many religions speak of providence, God at work in what happens, often in ways no one can see at the time. Those are beliefs, held by serious people for a very long time, and no experiment can settle them. And here's the part that works either way. Why did this happen? often has no answer you can reach. What now? always does. Whether or not there's a reason built in, there's a meaning you can make with what comes next.
screen: `WHY ARE ROCKS POINTY?` · `NATURE DOES NOTHING IN VAIN.` · `PROVIDENCE: AN OLD BELIEF.` · `NOT WHY, BUT WHAT NOW.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Bring to mind one thing from this year you still can't explain. Don't try to. Breathe in with it. As you breathe out, let the question turn from why to what now. No answer needed yet.
Meant to be. A feeling nearly every mind makes, and, for many people, a belief. First word on your strand.
screen: `MEANT TO BE — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line: not why, but what now. It works whatever you believe about the why. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People make sense of hard events in many ways: through faith in providence, through Stoic or Buddhist reflection, or simply by asking what to do next. Counselors often help people find meaning after a loss without asking them to believe the loss was planned.

match.prompt: where the feeling comes from — tap the pairs.
pairs: God at work in what happens
the question that always has an answer

myth: Aristotle said everything happens for a reason
the line isn't in his writing. he said nature does nothing in vain: an eye is for seeing.
in one set of studies, many atheists also said life events happened for a reason
believers said it more often, but the feeling isn't only religious.
an experiment has settled whether there's a plan behind events
that's a belief no experiment can settle. what's been studied is why we feel it.

fork.setup: young kids are asked why rocks are pointy: because of how they formed, or so animals can scratch on them. what do many of them pick?
options: so animals can scratch on them.
fork.reveal: the animals. minds reach for purpose first. adults do it too, just about bigger things.

original.note: Greek, telos: an end, a purpose. Aristotle's word for what a thing is for; English teleology comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fact about the universe, or a line from Aristotle.
what it means: a feeling almost every mind makes, and, for many, a belief in providence.
what a scholar hears: Kelemen's work on children's 'promiscuous teleology'; Banerjee and Bloom (2014) on believers and atheists; Aristotle's 'nature does nothing in vain' (Politics 1.2).

story.title: the farmer's horse
story.text: A farmer's only horse runs off across the border, and his neighbors say what bad luck. Maybe, says the farmer. Months later the horse comes back, bringing a fine horse from the other side, and the neighbors say what good luck. Maybe. His son rides the new horse, falls, and breaks his leg. Then war comes, the young men of the village are sent to fight, and the boy with the broken leg stays home.
story.source: a Chinese parable from the Huainanzi (2nd century BCE), chapter 18; retold in many versions

wrong.myth: Aristotle said everything happens for a reason.
wrong.truth: he didn't. he said nature does nothing in vain, about how living things are built. nobody knows who said the popular line first.

build.prompt: put the farmer's year in order.

think.setup: a friend's relationship just ended, and someone tells her everything happens for a reason. she looks worse. what might help more?
options: agree with them: it was meant to be.
say: i'm here. that sounds so hard.
list everything that was wrong with him.
think.reveal: the line can comfort the person who chooses it. offered to someone hurting, it can sound like their pain was the plan. company first; meaning can come later.

games.betReveal: it's a feeling nearly every mind makes, believers and not. no famous text says the line. what you make of what happens next is yours.

sources.ref: Kelemen, "Why are rocks pointy? Children's preference for teleological explanations of the natural world," Developmental Psychology 35 (1999)
Banerjee & Bloom, "Does everything happen for a reason?" Cognition 133 (2014)
Aristotle, Politics 1.2 (1253a9) and De Anima 3.9 (nature does nothing in vain)
Stoic providence (e.g. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 2; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations)
Huainanzi 18 (the old man at the frontier who lost his horse)
"Why we think that everything happens for a reason," Psychology Today (2018); Big Think on the same question

notes: New lesson (2026-10-06), written from docs/learning/AUDIENCE_RESEARCH_SPIRITUAL.md (Top 20 #1, proposed day 1).

Kelemen 1999: children chose between a physical explanation and a purpose explanation for pointy rocks (e.g. so animals could scratch on them); confirm the item wording and that 'many picked the animals' is fair to the result.

Banerjee & Bloom 2014: believers and, to a lesser degree, atheists reported that significant life events happened for a reason; the tendency tracked mentalizing (reading intentions). The script says 'a surprising number of atheists' and glosses the mentalizing link plainly; confirm.
The popular line is not in Aristotle's surviving works; 'nature does nothing in vain' is Politics 1.2 (1253a9), also De Anima 3.9 and elsewhere. Confirm no stronger attribution exists.

Providence is described as a belief held by many religions, without saying it is false; the 'works either way' turn is meant to sit well with believers and non-believers alike. Keeper to confirm the tone.
Story: Huainanzi 18 (塞翁失马). The second horse is 'a fine horse of the Hu' (nomads); the son's injury is to the leg/hip; most young men at the border died in the war. Told lightly; confirm.
